summary: We developed MarsWalk AR, a hyperlocal tactical navigation and science interface designed for astronauts conducting surface excursions (EVAs) on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater. While existing planetary tools focus on global views, MarsWalk AR addresses the challenge by layering four real NASA mission datasets—MRO HiRISE/CTX optical imagery, Curiosity’s actual traverse path, MGS TES thermal inertia maps, and MRO CRISM mineral scans—into one unified spacesuit tablet display. Using these layers, our system charts a suit-safe walking route from base camp to Mount Sharp’s boxwork formations (ancient groundwater mineral ridges), helping astronauts detour around loose Bagnold Dune sand traps, locate natural cliff overhangs for solar radiation shelter, and preview waypoints through 17 real Curiosity Mastcam "Street View" photos. This tool is vital because human explorers can delicately inspect and sample fragile geological formations that rovers cannot—turning complex multi-mission NASA data into real-time astronaut safety and scientific discovery.
details: MarsWalk AR: Tactical EVA Planner is a hyperlocal spacesuit navigation and science interface designed for astronauts conducting surface excursions (EVAs) on Mount Sharp in Gale Crater (4.59° S, 137.44° E). While existing planetary mapping platforms focus on global views for researchers on Earth, MarsWalk AR overlays four authentic NASA datasets into a live spacesuit HUD. It combines MRO HiRISE and CTX optical imagery for meter-scale boulder visibility, MSL Curiosity’s traverse telemetry as a ground-verified safe corridor around the dark Bagnold Dunes, MGS TES thermal inertia to separate heat-retaining solid bedrock from loose sand traps, and MRO CRISM mineral scans to highlight water-altered sulfates and silica in bright cyan and purple. Along the route, clickable waypoints pair orbital maps with 17 real Curiosity Mastcam "Street View" photographs (Sols 1–4700), allowing astronauts to preview terrain hazards, locate cliff radiation shelters, inspect legacy rover hardware, and sample fragile boxwork mineral ridges while monitoring real-time oxygen, battery, wind, and radiation limits. The primary benefits and intended impact of MarsWalk AR centre on astronaut safety, scientific efficiency, and future mission scalability. By detecting loose sand traps, steep slopes (>15°), and solar storm shelters in real time, the system keeps surface crews safe within strict four-hour spacesuit life-support budgets. Scientifically, it empowers human explorers to step delicately between fragile one-to-two-meter boxwork ridges that wheeled rovers risk crushing, enabling astronauts to map 3D mineral veins with handheld LiDAR and extract two intact core samples (1.5 kg) for Earth return. Beyond Gale Crater, its modular HUD architecture is designed to scale directly to future Artemis lunar excursions and any human landing site on Mars. To build MarsWalk AR, our team utilised NASA Mars Trek (trek.nasa.gov/mars) and the NASA Mars Science Laboratory (MSL) Raw Images Archive (mars.nasa.gov/msl), integrating orbital and surface datasets from MRO (HiRISE, CTX, CRISM), MGS (TES), MSL Curiosity (Mastcam, RAD, REMS), and regional ESA Mars Express HRSC context. We developed the interactive map layer toggles, waypoint popups, and HUD logic using JavaScript (assisted by Claude), designed the 15-slide spacesuit HUD and Team Poster in Canva, refined our mission documentation with Grammarly, and hosted our presentation materials via YouTube and Google Drive. Our project takes a creative approach by fusing orbital spectroscopy and thermal physics with chronological rover ground photography (Sols 1–4700) and a dynamic telemetry HUD that evolves across every stage of the walk. In designing the route, Team Martian Wayfinders carefully accounted for human mobility limits in pressurised spacesuits by detouring around 22° Bagnold Dune sand slopes, tracking consumable oxygen and battery reserves, establishing an eight-minute emergency shelter protocol under 15-meter Murray Buttes sandstone overhangs (~40% directional cosmic-ray shielding during simulated RAD solar alerts), and protecting fragile boxwork formations from accidental mechanical damage.
